transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-29 15:00 PST | Duration: ~52 mins
Attendees: Emma Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Martinez (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Fathom Head of AI), Ethan Rogers (Platform Engineer), Lucille Park (Product), Omar Aziz (CTO, joined at 15:28)

[00:00] Emma: Hey everybody, welcome thanks for taking the time. I'm Emma from Redwood, AE on this account. We've got Carlos from our SE team — he'll run through the demo bits. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Maya: Good thanks, excited — we want to see how your hosted API handles short retail conversational flows.
[00:10] Emma: Awesome. Quick agenda — 1) quick qual (stack, constraints), 2) live hosted API demo focusing on streaming and parameters, 3) retry/idempotency patterns, 4) Q&A and next steps. Sound ok?
[00:18] Lucille: Yep that works.
[00:20] Carlos: Alright I'm going to share my screen... uh small note, transcription might garble some names — sorry if you see "Redwood Optimeyes" in there, that's actually Redwood Optimize, haha.
[00:29] Carlos: So we call out two main paths — streaming responses for low-latency UX, and non-streamed for batch. For retail micro-responses (e.g., product quick answers) streaming is usually best.
[00:38] [00:38] Carlos: demo: hitting the hosted /v1/chat endpoint. Example prompt: "What's the return policy for item 5234?" You can see the server returns a first token within ~50ms in this sandbox, full message at ~180ms in this local trace.
[00:50] Ethan: Wait 50ms first token? That's, that seems optimistic — is that p50 or cold start?
[00:55] Carlos: Good call. This is warm p50 in our small sandbox. We'll need your traffic histogram to project 95p under load. Warm p95 in hosted for similar configs is typically in the 200-400ms range depending on model size.
[01:10] Maya: Our SLA ask is sub-350ms 95th for 1-2 sentence replies. Is that realistic without dedicated?
[01:15] Carlos: Possibly. Two levers: model selection (smaller, quantized variants) and batching configuration. Also routing policies — route by latency to GPU pools in the same region. If you need strict guarantees, Dedicated is the safer path, but hosted often meets tighter SLOs for many workloads.
[01:32] [01:32] Emma: Can I interject — cost wise dedicated has a higher fixed commitment but predictable per-token cost; hosted can be cheaper at low volume but variable.
[01:40] Lucille: And what's the fallback if a hosted node gets overloaded?
[01:44] Carlos: Automatic fallback — our smart routing will try compatible model variants, and we have graceful degradation options like returning truncated answers or cached prefixes. For chat we also have KV cache — uh sometimes the transcript calls it "K V cash" — but it's the same idea; prefix caching avoids regenerating the same context.
[02:00] [02:00] Carlos: Now I'm going to demo parameter effects — temp, top_p, max_tokens, and stop sequences. Watch how increasing temperature drives more diverse text and slightly longer generation time.
[02:12] [02:12] Carlos: Example: temp 0.0 deterministic short answer: "You can return within 30 days with receipt." Returned in X tokens, cheaper. Temp 0.9 gives more verbose answers and occasionally hedging language — costs more tokens and slightly higher latency.
[02:30] Maya: For our use case we prefer concise deterministic answers — sounds like temp 0-0.2.
[02:35] Carlos: That matches most retail assistants. Also note top_p interacts with temperature; you can tune to reduce hallucination while keeping low variance.
[02:44] [02:44] Ethan: How do retries factor in? If our client retries after a 500 or timeout, won't that double bill?
[02:49] Carlos: Great question. We recommend an idempotency key on generation requests so the platform can dedupe repeated requests. Retries that include the same idempotency key within a short window will be de-duplicated; you'll only be billed once. If the retry has a different key, yes you'll be billed again.
[03:05] Emma: Also retry strategies: exponential backoff with jitter, and client-side idempotency are the pattern. Server also returns a retry-after header for throttling.
[03:14] [03:14] Maya: Is there an SDK helper for idempotency?
[03:17] Carlos: Yes, our SDKs include a request helper you can use to generate and attach idempotency keys. We'll share code snippets.
[03:22] [03:22] Lucille: Data residency — our users are in EU and US. We need audit logs and to ensure customer data doesn't cross regions. Does hosted support region pinning?
[03:29] Carlos: Yes hosted supports region selection per request and we capture audit logs and request-level metadata. For stronger guarantees we offer Private (VPC) where the control plane is customer-local; if you need on-prem we also have a private package.
[03:42] [03:42] Ethan: On the VPC note, is there a networking handshake or egress IP allowlist?
[03:46] Carlos: We support both approaches — TLS and peered VPCs for Private; for hosted we can provide static egress IP ranges for allowlisting.
[03:53] [03:53] Emma: I'm going to run a quick live pattern that shows a failure mode — simulated transient GPU OOM leading to 502. Observe how the client sees a short-lived error and how our retry + fallback to smaller model returns a response.
[04:05] [04:05] Carlos: demo continued: request hits primary model, 502 -> automatic fallback to a smaller quantized variant. The client receives partial stream then a final message.
[04:18] Maya: In production we'd rather a slower response than a degraded answer. Is there a way to prefer increased latency over shorter gen?
[04:22] Carlos: Yes you can adjust fallback policy in routing: prefer model variants with higher latency tolerance, set max-burst and queue depth. Also you can set an SLO-based policy: if latency > threshold, return cached short answer.
[04:34] [04:34] Ethan: Billing question — if we fall back to a bigger model, how is cost reported?
[04:38] Emma: We show token-level cost per route in the console and in the billing export. You can attribute cost to route/model and even token type.
[04:45] [04:45] Lucille: Can we see the console?
[04:47] Carlos: Sure — quick screen share of Console -> Models -> Routes. Here you can see per-route latency distribution, token cost, and a sample trace. The trace shows event markers (prefetch, prefix-cache hit, generation start).
[04:59] [04:59] Maya: Nice. Do you keep long-term conversation logs by default? We need short retention for compliance.
[05:04] Carlos: Retention is configurable per workspace; default is 90 days but we can set down to 7 and integrate with your KMS for encrypted logs.
[05:11] [05:11] Lucille: About metrics: will we get percentiles and broken-down tokens per prompt?
[05:15] Carlos: Yes — Console provides p50/p95/p99, token breakdown, and per-token latency estimates. We also provide export to your observability tool via tracing hooks.
[05:24] [05:24] Ethan: Ok real-world constraints — we plan to start with hosted for speed-to-market. What traffic volume should push us to Dedicated?
[05:31] Emma: A few signals: sustained peak throughput that saturates routing pools, or strict latency SLOs tied to revenue. Typical threshold customers move to Dedicated around sustained tens of thousands of peak QPS or when they need hardware isolation. But we always recommend an analysis with your histogram.
[05:47] [05:47] Maya: Understood. For POC, we'd do 2-3 week sandbox testing with 10k MAUs, lower concurrency initial.
[05:54] [05:54] Carlos: Perfect — as next steps we'll run a projection: you give us the histogram and we map to models, expected p95 latencies and estimated monthly token cost.
[06:02] [06:02] Omar (joined): Sorry I'm late — quick question, how are secrets / API keys rotated? We use KMS across cloud providers.
[06:09] Carlos: We integrate with AWS KMS and other KMS providers; keys can be rotated and we support customer-managed keys on Private. For hosted we offer envelope encryption and audit logs.
[06:19] Emma: Quick recap, we'll send: benchmark sheet, sample SDK snippets for idempotency, a short checklist for networking/VPC options, and propose a POC scoping meeting.
[06:29] [06:29] Maya: Sounds good.
[06:31] Emma: Any last questions?
[06:33] Lucille: One more on model version pinning — if you pin a model and Redwood updates the underlying variant, do we get automatic upgrades?
[06:39] Carlos: No automatic upgrades for pinned versions. You control rollouts; we support canary and A/B tests through the console.
[06:46] Maya: Great. Thank you both.
[06:48] Emma: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the sheet and schedule.

End transcript.

Notes on transcription artifacts: occasional mis-hears ("K V cash" for KV cache, "Redwood Optimeyes" instead of Redwood Optimize), punctuation is messy in places, and speaker labels for the late joiner were added retroactively.
